result.summary: Menelaus kills Euphorbus and defends the body of Patroclus, but Hector, urged on by Apollo and Jove, puts on Achilles' armour and rallies the Trojans. Ajax and others fight to save the body, Jove pities Achilles' horses, and Menelaus sends Antilochus to tell Achilles while the body is carried toward the ships.

scenes.title: Menelaus kills Euphorbus
scenes.summary: Menelaus stands over Patroclus, kills Euphorbus, and is confronted by Hector, whom Apollo rouses.
scenes.stakes: Menelaus risks his life and the body of Patroclus falling to the Trojans.

scenes.title: Hector takes Achilles' armour
scenes.summary: Menelaus yields the body and fetches Ajax; Glaucus rebukes Hector, who dons Achilles' armour and rallies the allies.
scenes.stakes: Hector's doom is sealed by wearing Achilles' armour; the Greeks risk losing Patroclus' body.

scenes.title: The great struggle over the body
scenes.summary: Greek chiefs rally; Ajax kills Hippothous and Phorcys; Apollo rouses Aeneas; the battle rages in darkness all day.
scenes.stakes: The body of Patroclus may be dragged off and mutilated; many heroes may die.

scenes.title: Achilles' horses and Automedon
scenes.summary: Achilles is ignorant of the death; his horses weep and Jove revives them; Automedon and Alcimedon fight and Automedon kills Aretus.
scenes.stakes: Automedon risks death or loss of the immortal horses to Hector and Aeneas.

scenes.title: Minerva and Jove turn the tide
scenes.summary: Minerva heartens Menelaus; Apollo urges Hector; Jove sends darkness and gives the Trojans victory until Ajax prays and light returns.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans face rout and loss of Patroclus' body.

scenes.title: Bearing the body away
scenes.summary: Menelaus sends Antilochus to Achilles, and he and Meriones carry Patroclus off while the Ajaxes cover the retreat.
scenes.stakes: Failure means the corpse is lost and the Achaeans routed.

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is an epithet of Apollo.
Apollo takes the form of Mentes, chief of the Cicons.

notable_quotes.reason: Menelaus' proverb that a fool is wise after the event.
Achilles' immortal horses weep for Patroclus, a moving moment.
Ajax's prayer: if we must die, let it be in daylight.

analysis.text: The book shows loyalty and honour in defending a fallen comrade's body, while divine will shifts fortunes.
Treatment of corpses mattered greatly in Homeric culture; denial of burial or mutilation was a dire insult.

legacy.text: Homeric similes in this book, such as the lion defending its cubs, influenced later epic poets including Virgil.

fun_facts.text: The book is a classic example of Homer's extended similes, drawing on lions, boars, and herdsmen from everyday life.

language_notes.text: "Bestride" means to stand over a fallen man with legs on either side, shielding him from attackers.
"Pard" is an old word for the leopard or panther.
Hyperenor was a Trojan, Euphorbus's brother, whom Menelaus had earlier killed in battle; Euphorbus later cites this death as his grievance.
A proverb: a fool understands only after the harm is done. Menelaus warns Euphorbus not to learn this way.
"Vaunted" means boasted.
The Graces were goddesses of beauty and charm, so the comparison marks Euphorbus's hair as exceptionally lovely.
Apollo, favouring Troy, disguises himself as Mentes, leader of the Cicons, a Thracian people allied with Troy.
The horses of Achilles (son of Aeacus's line) were immortal gifts to his father Peleus; Hector hopes to capture them. Achilles' mother is the sea goddess Thetis.
"Cry shame upon me" means to publicly reproach or disgrace me for abandoning Patroclus's body.
"In despite of heaven" means in defiance of the gods; "rue" means to regret bitterly.
"Hue and cry" is the shouting of a pursuing crowd; "stockyard" is the cattle enclosure the lion raided.
Ilius is another name for Ilium, that is Troy; "citadel" is its fortified high point.
Sarpedon, the Lycian leader and Jove's son, was killed by Patroclus; his body was defended by the Lycians, and Glaucus charges Hector with abandoning it.
The armour was given to Peleus by the gods at his wedding to Thetis; Patroclus had borrowed it, and Achilles himself will die young.
"Reck" means to heed or take notice of; Hector pays no heed to his coming death.
"Bowed his portentous brows" is Jove's nod of assent, which makes a decision binding; here it seals Hector's fate.
"Drink at the public cost" means the leaders are honored guests entitled to wine at the community's expense, a mark of rank.
"Severally" means individually, one by one.
"Esquire" means squire or attendant in arms; Meriones is Idomeneus' companion and charioteer-fighter.
"Descendant of Aeacus" is a way of naming Achilles, whose grandfather was Aeacus.
"Bestridden" means standing astride the body to guard it, or here to seize it.
"Pelasgian" refers to an old people of Greece, here allied with Troy.
"Never repaid his parents the cost of bringing him up" refers to the Greek idea that sons owed their parents care in old age.
Antilochus is Nestor's son; Nestor sent him and Thrasymedes to fight, so they are unaware of Patroclus' death far across the field.
Achilles' mother is the sea-goddess Thetis; she had told him Troy would not fall through him alone.
"Descendant of Aeacus" means Achilles, grandson of Aeacus; his horses are immortal gifts to his father Peleus.
"Upbraid" means to scold or reproach.
The armour is Achilles', which Patroclus wore and Hector stripped from his body after killing him.
"Scatheless" means unharmed.
"Lies on the lap of heaven" means the outcome rests with the gods.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war; his robbing the spear of force means it stopped quivering.
The bow is the rainbow, which Jove sets in the sky as a portent, here of war or storm.
"Vouchsafe" means to graciously grant.
"Girdle" here means the belt guarding the waist and lower body.
The aegis is Jove's tasselled shield or cloak; shaking it spreads terror and storm. Ida is the mountain near Troy where he watches.
Coiranus saved Idomeneus by driving up to him, and so took the spear meant for another and died.
"Hitherwards" means toward this place.
Ajax asks only for daylight, even if the gods will his death: he wants to die fighting in the open.
"Straitly" is archaic for strictly or sternly; he gave them a firm charge.
The narrator suddenly addresses Menelaus directly ("O Menelaus"), a Homeric habit used for characters he favors.
Danaans, Argives and Achaeans are interchangeable names for the Greeks in this translation.
"One in heart as in name": both warriors are called Ajax (Ajax son of Telamon and Ajax son of Oileus), and they fight as a pair.
"Hue and cry" means a loud shout of pursuit; "loo" is an old form of lee, meaning shelter or rear.
"Spears pointed at both the ends" describes spears with a point at each end, one for thrusting and one to stick upright in the ground.

context_notes.text: Patroclus, Achilles' close friend, has just been killed after fighting in Achilles' armour; both sides now struggle over his body and its armour.
Euphorbus had indeed first wounded Patroclus with a spear, before Hector finished him. Winning spoils and glory by claiming the kill mattered greatly to heroes.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and guardian of oaths and proper conduct, so Menelaus appeals to him.
Ajax son of Telamon is the greatest Greek warrior after Achilles, famed for his huge body-covering shield.
Mutilating and exposing a corpse to dogs was a grave dishonour, denying the dead proper burial rites.
Dardanians are Trojans descended from Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojan royal line.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war; his entering Hector means Hector is filled with battle fury.
Patroclus is Achilles' close friend, killed by Hector. Leaving a corpse to scavengers was a terrible dishonor for a Greek hero.
Apollo supports Troy. Gods often disguise themselves as mortals in the Iliad to speak to heroes.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is god of war, and Minerva (Athena) a goddess of war and strategy.
Achilles is sulking by the ships, so he has not yet learned of Patroclus' death.
The son of Saturn is Jove (the Greek Zeus), king of the gods, who pities the immortal horses.
Automedon is Achilles' and Patroclus' charioteer, so he is praised for knowing how to handle the divine horses.
Aeneas is a leading Trojan, son of Anchises and the goddess Venus.
Phoenix is Achilles' aged tutor and companion. Minerva borrows his form to speak with authority to Menelaus.
Apollo supported the Trojans throughout the poem and often takes a mortal's form to rouse Hector.
Meriones is Idomeneus' companion and fellow Cretan commander. Lyctus is a city in Crete.
Achilles is sulking by his ships and not fighting, so he has not yet heard that Patroclus, wearing his armour, has died.
Hector stripped Patroclus of the armour of Achilles, which Patroclus had borrowed to fight in Achilles' place.
Pylians are the men of Nestor's kingdom of Pylos, whom Antilochus, Nestor's son, had been leading in battle.
Aeneas, son of Anchises, is a leading Trojan warrior, said to be a favourite of the gods.

literary_notes.text: Menelaus is compared to a cow protecting her first calf, stressing his fierce protectiveness and tenderness toward the fallen Patroclus.
The young olive tree, flourishing then flattened by a storm, mirrors Euphorbus's promise and sudden death, adding pathos to the stripping of his armour.
Menelaus is likened to a lion feeding on a heifer, with cowering dogs and shepherds showing how terrifying he is.
Hector's advance is compared to a flame, suggesting destructive speed and intensity as he enters the fight.
Menelaus's reluctant retreat is compared to a lion driven from a stockyard, showing both his courage and his unwilling withdrawal.
Ajax is likened to a lion guarding its cubs, conveying fierce protectiveness; the lion image now contrasts with Menelaus's retreat.
The remark that the son did not grow old in his father's armour reminds us of Achilles's early death.
Jove predicts that Hector will never return to Andromache, foretelling his death at Achilles's hands.
The narrator calls the Trojans fools; readers know Ajax will kill many, while the Trojans hope for victory.
The Trojan charge is compared to a huge wave crashing on rocks, conveying noise and force.
Ajax is likened to a boar scattering hounds and hunters, stressing his fierce, stubborn strength.
Noting that Hippothous died far from home and never repaid his parents stirs sympathy for a minor warrior.
The darkness around the fighters against bright daylight elsewhere makes this struggle seem uniquely grim and set apart.
The tug-of-war over an ox-hide being stretched shows the two armies hauling the corpse back and forth.
We know Patroclus is dead while Achilles does not, building tension for the moment he learns.
The motionless grieving horses are compared to a gravestone pillar, stressing their fixed mourning.
The horses weep and mourn like humans, showing the depth of loss.
Automedon is a vulture among geese, showing his fierce yet fruitless attack.
The narrator calls the Trojans fools, hinting their hopes will fail.
The slaughter of an ox shows Aretus' sudden bound and collapse.
Comparing the bloodied Automedon to a gorged lion emphasizes his savagery.
Minerva's descent is compared to the rainbow, a bright sign of coming war or storm, foreshadowing the renewed fighting.
The fly, persistent and greedy for blood, makes an unheroic comparison that conveys Menelaus' stubborn courage.
The graphic detail of teeth and tongue makes the violence of Hector's spear vivid and shocking.
Ajax addresses Jove directly, a plain, moving prayer that shows his courage and also his helplessness.
Menelaus' reluctant retreat is likened to a lion driven off by herdsmen, hounds and brands, extended at length.
Menelaus' searching gaze is compared to an eagle spotting a hare, an extended comparison that stresses his sharpness and urgency.
The very short sentence conveys the shock of Patroclus' death and Antilochus' grief with little elaboration.
The Trojans are like hounds menacing a boar that turns on them, showing how the Ajaxes' fury makes pursuers shrink back.
Battle is likened to a city-consuming fire, conveying the overwhelming roar and destruction around the bearers.
Mules hauling timber compare to the bearers' exertion, giving the strain of carrying the body a homely, physical image.
The Ajaxes are likened to a wooded ridge holding back a river, making them an immovable barrier against the Trojan tide.
